claim: When freehand-tracing a symmetric silhouette against multiple reference views (front/side/top), instead of manually rotating one object between views repeatedly, make several Alt+D linked duplicates of the in-progress mesh, position/rotate each *duplicate object* to face a different reference view, and edit whichever one is currently easiest to see -- since linked duplicates share mesh data, every edit-mode change to any one of them appears on all the others simultaneously, so cross-checking silhouette accuracy from multiple angles becomes fast hopping between pre-positioned objects instead of repeated manual rotation.
supporting_evidence: Direct quote (~5:26-5:34): "what we can do is we can press alt D this will duplicate it and any changes we make to one are going to be adjusted to the other which is great so what I'm going to do is once again alt D can rotate this 90 degrees negative 90 rather... we're going to alt D this again and then r y 90 r y negative 90 to go upside down okay so now any changes I make you know are going to be adjusted to all these"
rejected_alternative: Manually rotating and re-positioning a single object between reference views repeatedly during blockout
reason: Repeated manual rotation between views is described as "just kind of like you know a pain"; pre-positioned linked duplicates eliminate that repeated setup cost for every single edit check.

claim: When a freehand-traced loop that should stay circular gets visibly distorted from manual vertex placement, use the LoopTools add-on's Circle or Relax operator to redistribute the vertices evenly -- Relax can be repeated with Shift+R until the loop settles into an even distribution; both operators will move vertices from their manually-placed positions, which is an accepted tradeoff for restoring even spacing.
supporting_evidence: Direct quote (~4:19-4:23, and reiterated ~9:07): "if you turn on the loop tools feature in the add-ons panel just search for Loop tools right click Loop tools and then Circle you can either use Circle or what might work better in this case is the relax feature what this does is it distributes the vertices evenly so I can press press shift r a few times to repeat that command"

claim: Pinching near a mesh boundary under Subdivision Surface is an inherent limitation, not necessarily a mistake -- a detail placed close to an edge will show more pinching the closer it is, and how much this matters is a judgment call, not something to always fully eliminate; check under more than one matcap/material since the severity can look different (worse or better) depending on lighting, before deciding whether it's worth fixing.
supporting_evidence: Direct quotes (~29:17-31:47): "in the reference photo this is pretty much right near the edge but if we do this with subd we're probably going to get some pinching... as for the pinching on this outer area it depends how much you want to worry about it this uh this could be a bit of an illusion with the mat cap... the closer this is to the edge the more of a pinching effect we're going to get... is this something I'd stress about not particularly... that's kind of one of the limitations of subd here"

claim: Reserve real modeled SubD/boolean geometry for primary and secondary shape-defining details only; tiny tertiary details (small buttons, logos, labels, decorative markings) should be represented with decals/textures instead of modeled geometry, matching standard game-asset production practice.
supporting_evidence: Direct quote (~26:14-26:30): "for these smaller details you could model these in or you could just use a decal if you were to use this in like as a game asset or something like that especially as a render modeling in these tiny details is just stupid every single game developer... are going to use decals for these tiny you know little tertiary details that's just what happens"
rejected_alternative: Modeling every small decorative detail (button icons, labels) as real geometry
reason: Modeling tiny tertiary details as real geometry is called out as wasted effort relative to the visual payoff; production workflows (game or render) represent them as decals/textures instead.

claim: Before applying a Subdivision Surface modifier's level irreversibly (which also converts a linked-duplicate mesh into a single-user copy, breaking the shared-edit link to its siblings), save a checkpoint first -- once applied, there is no way back to the lower-poly control cage except from that saved backup, since normal undo won't reliably restore it after other operations have followed.
supporting_evidence: Direct quote (~27:33-28:31): "at this point do another power save just to be safe and if I apply this with one level... make data single user apply modify yeah that's fine we'll go ahead and click apply there... this doesn't carry over with the alt D command doesn't matter though... you know we can't really undo this right we can't go back to that low poly State unless we made a duplicate or have a previous save so always make backup saves"

claim: When freehand-tracing an organic-ish silhouette from reference, deliberately work at a very low vertex/segment count first and get the overall proportions and quad connectivity right at that low resolution, rather than tracing at high detail immediately -- reconnecting mismatched high vertex counts across different traced sections is significantly harder than reconnecting a simplified, condensed version, and support/proximity loops should only be added once the low-poly blockout is confirmed correct.
supporting_evidence: Direct quote (~19:20-20:00): "this is where things are probably going to a little get a little bit messy... reason being is because we have a lot more vertices here than we have to connect up here so technically what I would need to do is add some additional Loops but this is going to cause issues so what I'd actually like to do instead is condense this down to an even lower resolution... it should be easier to connect everything up now hopefully"
rejected_alternative: Continuing to trace and connect the mismatched sections at their original higher vertex counts
reason: Reconciling two independently-traced sections with different vertex counts is harder than simplifying both down to a shared low resolution first and reconnecting from there.
